newsitem.title: UK: Buoyant Britain savours brave new world.
newsitem.headline: Buoyant Britain savours brave new world.

text.p: Staid old Britain is behaving in a thoroughly unstaid way.
People are smiling in public.
The sun is out.
And there is a groundswell of community and togetherness in a country that values individuality and privacy above all.
A new era has dawned.
"The future starts here. We will remember these days for the rest of our lives," said Britain's best-selling Sun newspaper.
Eighteen years of Conservative rule ended on Thursday when the government was routed in an overwhelming endorsement of Tony Blair's centrist, new-look Labour Party.
The nation, collectively, chose to slap the Conservatives in the face and punish them for perceived weak leadership, sleaze and years of divisive and divided rule.
An experienced democracy, Britain finally learnt the art of tactical voting, rising against the government with such venom that Scotland and Wales became Conservative-free zones.
To be sure, there is relief that the end of a tiresome six-week election campaign coincides with the arrival of spring.
There are also plenty of Conservatives who are aghast to see their party reduced to a sorry sliver of its old self.
But most of all, there is optimism in a country usually loath to look on the bright side of life.

"Tony Blair has fired the country's imagination. He has captured its mood for a fresh start and sparked a revolution of rising expectations. He has turned party politics on its head," said the Sun, once the staunchest of Conservative supporters.

As it dawned on Britain that Labour had secured a crushing 179-strong majority -- despite Blair's prediction that Britain had no taste for landslides -- crowds thronged to Downing Street on Friday to welcome in the new man and his new era.
Strangers hugged strangers, Blair kissed old women and all but anointed young children in scenes of jubilation reminiscent of distant soccer victories and once-fairytale royal weddings.
Such euphoric times, of course, cannot last but the nation appeared hell bent on enjoying them while they did.

"I'm knackered, euphoric, shocked at the size of it all and ecstatic to see that lot finally go," said 26-year-old Raj Singh after a drink-sodden night of celebrations. "I don't think the full reality will actually sink in until Monday morning."

As Blair and his wife Cherie were propelled along by a throng of well-wishers -- hands outstretched, flags aloft and voices raised -- Britain could be forgiven for thinking it had a Clinton or a Kennedy in its midst, not a British prime minister.
The U.S. language of hope also pervaded Blair's first speech as prime minister, with lofty talk of partnership and trust in a united Britain fit for the millennium.
Not just a new party but a new generation seized power as 43-year-old Blair became Britain's youngest leader this century.
A record number of women were elected to parliament, along with fresh-faced, fresh-thinking MPs in their 20s, Britain's first Moslem MP, twins, sisters, a mother-and-son team...

In the Cabinet, a blind man was chosen to put the nation's schools to rights and for the first time, openly gay men were ushered into the political mainstream. Blair has big shoes to fill with his oft-stated promise of "new Labour, new Britain".
"So huge was his performance that it has given rise to massive hopes and dreams, far exceeding what he promised in order to secure his victory," wrote Hugo Young in the Guardian.
"It is as if a huge burden has been lifted off the nation's back," Young wrote. "The election cleans out the House. But it also purges, for a while, national pessimism."
Yet alongside the uplifted, the letter page of the Daily Telegraph revealed the despair of the vanquished, embodied in the plans of one P.J. Bridgwood of Templecombe in Somerset.
"Sir -- the electorate has made its bed; it must lie in it. I am off to France on the ferry. God Help Britain."
